items.title: Focus Question: Why does a firefighter holding a high-pressure hose get pushed backward, and how is that related to recoil?

answer.html: Recoil is the backward motion of an object when it throws something forward (a firefighter's hose throwing water, a gun firing, a rocket expelling gas). Momentum is conserved, so the water thrown forward and the hose and firefighter pushed back have equal and opposite momenta. The same idea lets spacecraft accelerate with nothing to push against.

items.title: Revisit the Encounter the Phenomenon Question (Lesson 2): An astronaut floats motionless in space, away from her station, holding only a heavy wrench. How could she use what you learned in this lesson to start moving back toward the station?

answer.html: She can throw the wrench directly away from the station. The astronaut and wrench form a closed system with zero total momentum, so the wrench gets momentum away from the station and she gets equal momentum toward it. The heavier the wrench and the faster the throw, the faster she moves.

items.title: Figure 10, Analyze: Two lab carts, A and B, collide on a track. In the diagram the arrows for the force of A on B and the force of B on A are the same length and the contact time is the same for both carts. How can you tell the impulses have the same magnitude?

body.html: The change in momentum of each cart equals its impulse 𝐹𝛥𝑡. By Newton's third law the two forces are equal and opposite, and they act for the same time.

answer.html: The force arrows have the same length (Newton's third law) and act for the same time 𝛥𝑡, so the impulses 𝐹𝛥𝑡 are equal in size and opposite in direction.

check.html: Equal and opposite impulses give equal and opposite momentum changes, so the total momentum is unchanged.

items.title: 17 (Railcars): A 2.5 × 105-kg railcar moving at 1.6 m/s couples with a 1.5 × 105 -kg railcar at rest. What is their speed after they stick together?

body.html: 𝑚<sub>1</sub> = 2.5 × 10<sup>5</sup> kg, 𝑣<sub>1</sub><sub>𝑖</sub>= + 1.6 m/s, 𝑚<sub>2</sub> = 1.5 × 10<sup>5</sup> kg, 𝑣<sub>2</sub><sub>𝑖</sub>= 0. Find 𝑣<sub>𝑓</sub>.

The two cars form a closed, isolated system (no net external horizontal force), so momentum is conserved. In a perfectly inelastic collision, 𝑣<sub>1</sub><sub>𝑓</sub>= 𝑣<sub>2</sub><sub>𝑓</sub>= 𝑣<sub>𝑓</sub>.

answer.html: 1.0 m/s in the direction the first car was moving.

check.html: The total mass is 1.6 times the moving car's mass, so the speed drops to 1/1.6 of 1.6 m/s.

items.title: 18 (Lacrosse ball and goalie): A 0.140-kg lacrosse ball moving at 31 m/s is caught by a 72-kg goalie who is standing at rest on roller skates. How fast do the goalie and ball move together afterward?

body.html: 𝑚<sub>𝑏</sub>= 0.140 kg, 𝑣<sub>𝑏𝑖</sub>= 31 m/s, 𝑚<sub>𝑔</sub>= 72 kg, 𝑣<sub>𝑔𝑖</sub>= 0. Find 𝑣<sub>𝑓</sub>.
Conservation of momentum for the ball + goalie system; they move together afterward.

answer.html: 0.060 m/s (6.0 cm/s) in the ball's original direction.

check.html: Tiny ball, big goalie, so a tiny recoil speed.

items.title: 19 (Pellet and target): A 15.0-g pellet moving at 285 m/s strikes a 1.2-kg target at rest on a frictionless surface. The pellet bounces straight back at 12 m/s. What is the target's speed after the hit?

body.html: 𝑚<sub>𝑝</sub>= 0.0150 kg, 𝑣<sub>𝑝𝑖</sub>= + 285 m/s, 𝑣<sub>𝑝𝑓</sub>= −12 m/s, 𝑚<sub>𝑡</sub>= 1.2 kg, 𝑣<sub>𝑡𝑖</sub>= 0. Find 𝑣<sub>𝑡𝑓</sub>.
Momentum is conserved for the pellet + target system.
𝑣<sub>𝑡𝑓</sub>=

answer.html: 3.7 m/s in the pellet's original direction.

check.html: The target moves forward; because the pellet bounced back, the target receives more than 𝑚<sub>𝑝</sub>𝑣<sub>𝑝𝑖</sub> alone.

items.title: 20 (Challenge: head-on balls): A 0.80-kg ball moving at 5.0 m/s collides head-on with a 1.20-kg ball moving the opposite way at 8.0 m/s. After the collision the 0.80-kg ball moves backward (reverses) at 9.0 m/s. Find the velocity of the 1.20-kg ball.

body.html: Take the 0.80-kg ball's initial direction as +. 𝑚<sub>1</sub> = 0.80 kg, 𝑣<sub>1</sub><sub>𝑖</sub>= + 5.0 m/s, 𝑣<sub>1</sub><sub>𝑓</sub>= −9.0 m/s; 𝑚<sub>2</sub> = 1.20 kg, 𝑣<sub>2</sub><sub>𝑖</sub>= −8.0 m/s. Find 𝑣<sub>2</sub><sub>𝑓</sub>.
Conservation of momentum (signs matter).

answer.html: 1.3 m/s in the positive direction, which is the direction the 0.80-kg ball was originally moving (the 1.20-kg ball has reversed).

check.html: Initial momentum = 4.0 −9.6 = −5.6; final = −7.2 + 1.6 = −5.6 kg·m/s. Matches.

items.title: Figure 11, Infer: Two skaters stand at rest on ice, face to face, and push apart. A man moves 1.5 m to the east in the same time that a woman moves 2.4 m to the west. How can you tell from the motion which has the larger mass, and what is the ratio of their masses?

body.html: After the push, 𝑚<sub>𝑀</sub>𝑣<sub>𝑀</sub>= 𝑚<sub>𝑊</sub>𝑣<sub>𝑊</sub> in size (equal and opposite momenta). In the same time, the distances are in the same ratio as the speeds, so 𝑚<sub>𝑀</sub>/ 𝑚<sub>𝑊</sub>= 𝑣<sub>𝑊</sub>/ 𝑣<sub>𝑀</sub>= 𝑑<sub>𝑊</sub>/ 𝑑<sub>𝑀</sub>.

answer.html: The woman moves farther in the same time, so her speed is larger. Since their momenta are equal in size, the man has the larger mass, about 1.6 times hers.

check.html: The one who moves less has the greater mass.

items.title: Systems and System Models (Crosscutting Concepts): Two lab carts are pushed apart by a spring on a level track. A bright flag taped to the track stays in place. How does the flag help you analyze the carts as a system, and what model would you draw?

body.html: To use conservation of momentum, define the system and measure velocities relative to a frame that is not accelerating. The flag on the track gives a fixed reference position.

The flag lets you measure how far each cart moves from the start point at equal time intervals (by video), so you can find each cart's velocity. Model: a diagram with both carts as the system (dashed boundary), 𝑝<sub>before</sub> = 0, and arrows after the push for →𝑝<sub>1</sub> and →𝑝<sub>2</sub> of equal length pointing opposite ways.

answer.html: The flag provides a fixed reference so you can measure each cart's displacement and therefore its speed. A tape-measure grid or motion detector would also work. The model: system = both carts, total momentum zero before and after, with equal and opposite momentum arrows.

check.html: The two arrows sum to zero, as they must.

items.title: Get It? (Lesson 2, "Propulsion in Space"): A balloon "rocket" zips across a gym when you let go of the open end. Would it still work in a vacuum? Explain.

answer.html: Yes. The balloon and the air inside form a closed system. Air rushes out the opening backward, so the air gains backward momentum, and by conservation of momentum (and Newton's third law) the balloon gains an equal forward momentum. No outside air or surface is needed.

check.html: Same idea as a rocket expelling gas; the air in the room is not what pushes it.

items.title: 21 (Model rocket): A model rocket has a mass of 2.50 kg (not counting the gas it expels). At rest in space, it expels 35.0 g of burned fuel at 480 m/s. Find the rocket's velocity after the fuel burns (ignore gravity and air).

body.html: 𝑚<sub>𝑟</sub>= 2.50 kg, 𝑚<sub>𝑔</sub>= 0.0350 kg, 𝑣<sub>𝑔𝑓</sub>= −480 m/s (backward), initial momentum = 0.
Momentum conservation, as with an astronaut and a gas pistol: 0 = 𝑚<sub>𝑟</sub>𝑣<sub>𝑟</sub>+ 𝑚<sub>𝑔</sub>𝑣<sub>𝑔</sub>.

answer.html: 6.72 m/s in the direction opposite to the exhaust (forward).

check.html: Direction opposite to the gas; speed much less than 480 m/s since the rocket is much heavier.

items.title: 22 (Two carts and a spring): A spring pushes apart a 3.2-kg cart and a 1.6-kg cart that start at rest tied together. The 1.6-kg cart moves at 3.6 m/s to the right. What is the velocity of the 3.2-kg cart?

body.html: Right is +. 𝑚<sub>1</sub> = 1.6 kg, 𝑣<sub>1</sub><sub>𝑓</sub>= + 3.6 m/s, 𝑚<sub>2</sub> = 3.2 kg. Initial momentum 0.
Conservation of momentum for the two carts (the spring force is internal).
0 = 𝑚<sub>1</sub>𝑣<sub>1</sub><sub>𝑓</sub>+ 𝑚<sub>2</sub>𝑣<sub>2</sub><sub>𝑓</sub>

answer.html: 1.8 m/s to the left (opposite the 1.6-kg cart).

check.html: The cart twice as heavy moves at half the speed.

items.title: 23 (Challenge: raft): A 56.0-kg swimmer dives horizontally from a raft at 3.2 m/s forward. The raft with its other passenger (combined mass 130 kg) was at rest. What are the speed and direction of the raft right after the dive?

body.html: Forward is +. 𝑚<sub>𝑆</sub>= 56.0 kg, 𝑣<sub>𝑆𝑓</sub>= + 3.2 m/s, 𝑚<sub>𝑅</sub>= 130 kg (raft + passenger). Initial momentum 0 (the raft floats freely on the water).
Momentum conservation for swimmer + raft + passenger.
0 = 𝑚<sub>𝑆</sub>𝑣<sub>𝑆𝑓</sub>+ 𝑚<sub>𝑅</sub>𝑣<sub>𝑅𝑓</sub>

answer.html: 1.4 m/s backward (opposite to the swimmer's motion).

check.html: The swimmer is lighter than the raft plus passenger, so the raft's speed is lower than 3.2 m/s.

items.title: Figure 12, Analyze: Three marbles collide on a smooth tabletop and momentum is conserved. When the same collision is done on a table covered with coarse sandpaper, the total momentum of the marbles just after the collision is less than just before. Why is momentum of the three marbles not conserved on the sandpaper?

body.html: Momentum of a system is conserved only if the net external force is zero. Friction from the sandpaper is an external force on the marbles.

answer.html: Sandpaper friction exerts an external force on the marbles, so the three-marble system loses momentum. That momentum goes to the table and Earth, which gain an equal momentum in the opposite sense (a tiny change in velocity since Earth is so massive), so the momentum of the larger system (marbles + table + Earth) is conserved.

check.html: The marbles slow down and stop on the sandpaper; their lost momentum is exactly what the table and Earth gain.

items.title: 24 (North car and west car): A 1150-kg car moving north at 17.4 m/s collides with a 1520-kg car moving west at 11.6 m/s at an icy intersection. The cars stick together. Find their velocity (speed and direction) just after the collision.

body.html: North = +y, west = +x (so both components are positive). 𝑚<sub>𝑁</sub>= 1150 kg, 𝑣<sub>𝑁</sub>= 17.4 m/s, 𝑚<sub>𝑊</sub>= 1520 kg, 𝑣<sub>𝑊</sub>= 11.6 m/s; total mass 2670 kg. Find 𝑣<sub>𝑓</sub> and its direction.
Momentum is conserved separately along each axis; the final momentum is the vector sum.
𝑝<sup>𝑓</sup>= √𝑝<sup>𝑥</sup>

answer.html: 9.99 m/s, 48.6° north of west.

check.html: The north car had more momentum here, so the result points more north than west; the speed is below both initial speeds.

items.title: 25 (South car struck by east car): A 1240-kg car moving south at 9.7 m/s is struck by a 1810-kg car moving east at 24.6 m/s. The cars stick together. Find their velocity just after the collision.

body.html: East = +x, south = +y (down the page), total mass 3050 kg.
Same as above: add the momentum components.

answer.html: 15.1 m/s, 15.1° south of east.

check.html: Mostly eastward because the east-moving car has much more momentum.

items.title: 26 (Was the north-moving car speeding?): A 1120-kg car moving east at 13.9 m/s is struck by a 1640-kg car moving north. The cars stick together and move off at 10.6 m/s at an angle of 57.9° north of east. The speed limit is 13.4 m/s. Was the north- moving car speeding?

body.html: East = +x, north = +y. 𝑚<sub>𝐸</sub>= 1120 kg, 𝑣<sub>𝐸</sub>= 13.9 m/s, 𝑚<sub>𝑁</sub>= 1640 kg, 𝑣<sub>𝑓</sub>= 10.6 m/s, 𝜃= 57.9°, total mass 2760 kg. Find 𝑣<sub>𝑁</sub>.
The initial north momentum belongs only to the north car and must equal the final y- momentum.
Check with the x-direction: (2760)(10.6)cos57.9° = 1.55 × 10<sup>4</sup> and (1120)(13.9) = 1.56 × 10<sup>4</sup> kg·m/s. They agree.

answer.html: Yes. The north-moving car was going about 15 m/s, which exceeds the 13.4 m/s limit.

check.html: The x-momentum matches, so the given data are consistent.

items.title: 27 (Challenge: identical balls): A 0.16-kg ball moving at 3.2 m/s strikes an identical ball at rest. After the collision the moving ball leaves 35.0° to the left of its original direction, and the other ball leaves 55.0° to the right. Find the velocity of each ball.

body.html: 𝑚= 0.16 kg for both, 𝑣<sub>𝑖</sub>= 3.2 m/s along +x. Final angles: +35.0° (ball 1, left) and −55.0° (ball 2, right). Find 𝑣<sub>1</sub><sub>𝑓</sub>, 𝑣<sub>2</sub><sub>𝑓</sub>.
Conservation of momentum in x and y separately (the identical mass cancels).
y-direction (initial 𝑝<sub>𝑦</sub>= 0): 𝑣<sub>1</sub><sub>𝑓</sub>sin35.0° −𝑣<sub>2</sub><sub>𝑓</sub>sin55.0° = 0
x-direction: 𝑣<sub>𝑖</sub>= 𝑣<sub>1</sub><sub>𝑓</sub>cos35.0° + 𝑣<sub>2</sub><sub>𝑓</sub>cos55.0° = 𝑣<sub>1</sub><sub>𝑓</sub>(0.819 + 0.700 × 0.574) = 1.221 𝑣<sub>1</sub><sub>𝑓</sub>

answer.html: The ball originally moving: 2.6 m/s at 35.0° left of its original direction. The ball originally at rest: 1.8 m/s at 55.0° to the right.

check.html: Kinetic energy: 𝑣<sub>1</sub><sub>𝑓</sub>
<sup>2</sup> = 2.62<sup>2</sup> + 1.84<sup>2</sup> = 10.2 = 3.2<sup>2</sup>, so this collision is elastic and the energy is unchanged.

items.title: Figure 14, Decide: A toy gyroscope wheel is spinning fast with its axle horizontal and one end of the axle resting on a pivot post. The spinning wheel precesses (the axle swings slowly around in a horizontal circle), but an identical wheel that is not spinning just falls. Why?

body.html: Torque = (lever arm) × (force). The weight of the wheel acts at its center, away from the pivot, so there is a torque about the pivot. For the non-spinning wheel, → 𝐿= 0 at first, so the torque makes it rotate downward. For the spinning wheel, the torque is perpendicular to its large angular momentum → 𝐿.

answer.html: The torque from gravity changes
𝐿 in a direction perpendicular to
𝐿 itself, which turns the axle sideways (precession) instead of tipping it down. A non-spinning wheel has no angular momentum to turn, so the torque simply makes it fall.

check.html: A torque perpendicular to
𝐿 changes the direction of
𝐿 but not its size.

items.title: Get It? (Tops and Gyroscopes): Mars has a tilted axis and an equatorial bulge, and its axis precesses too. What causes it?

answer.html: Mars's equatorial bulge and tilted axis let the Sun's gravitational pull exert a small torque on the planet. Because Mars has large angular momentum, the torque slowly changes the direction of the axis (a very long cycle) rather than tipping the planet over.

check.html: Same mechanism as the tilted top and Earth's precession.

items.title: limit is 22 m/s. Your friend was driving the north car and says she was under the limit. (a) How fast was the north car going before the crash? (b) How fast was the west car going? Does the evidence support your friend's claim?

body.html: Axes +x east, +y north; the combined wreck moves 32° north of west. 𝑚<sup>𝑁</sup>= 1180 kg, 𝑚<sup>𝑊</sup>= 1470 kg, 𝑀= 2650 kg, skid distance 𝑑= 18.6 m, 𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>= 0.70, 𝑔= 9.80 m/s<sup>2</sup>. Find 𝑣<sub>𝑁</sub> and 𝑣<sub>𝑊</sub> before the crash.

(1) During the skid, friction is the only horizontal force: 𝑎= 𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>𝑔 and 𝑣<sup>2</sup> = 2𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>𝑔𝑑 gives the speed right after impact. (2) Momentum is conserved in the collision along each axis.
Speed just after the collision (skid to rest):
North momentum before = north momentum after: 𝑚<sub>𝑁</sub>𝑣<sub>𝑁</sub>= 𝑀𝑣sin32°
West momentum before = west momentum after: 𝑚<sub>𝑊</sub>𝑣<sub>𝑊</sub>= 𝑀𝑣cos32°

answer.html: Your friend (north car) was going about 19 m/s (19.0 m/s), under the 22 m/s limit.
The west car was going about 24 m/s (24.4 m/s), over the limit. Yes, the evidence supports your friend's claim: she was not speeding and the other driver was.

check.html: The west car has more mass and enough speed to have the larger momentum, which is why the wreck slides toward the west more than the north.

items.title: Check Your Progress, Problem 28 (Heavy-rim toy wheel): A toy gyro wheel has a thin, light disk with a thick, heavy metal rim. Why is it a good gyroscope?

body.html: Moment of inertia 𝐼= ∑𝑚𝑟<sup>2</sup> is large when mass is far from the axis. Angular momentum 𝐿= 𝐼𝜔.

answer.html: A heavy rim puts most of the mass far from the axis, giving a large moment of inertia. For a given spin rate the wheel has a large angular momentum, so it strongly resists changes in its spin axis and holds its orientation steadily.

check.html: Same idea as a spinning football or a flying disc with a heavy rim.

items.title: Check Your Progress, Problem 29 (Carts on a ramp): An 18.6-N cart is released from rest at the top of a 1.40-m long frictionless ramp tilted 25.0° above horizontal. At the bottom it strikes a 41.2-N cart that is at rest. (a) Find the speed of the first cart at the bottom. (b) Find the speed of both carts if they stick together.

body.html: Ramp length 1.40 m, angle 25.0°, cart 1 weighs 18.6 N, cart 2 weighs 41.2 N and is at rest at the bottom. Masses: 𝑚<sub>1</sub> = 18.6 / 9.80 = 1.90 kg, 𝑚<sub>2</sub> = 41.2 / 9.80 = 4.20 kg.

(a) On a frictionless incline, energy conservation gives <sub>12</sub>𝑚𝑣<sup>2</sup> = 𝑚𝑔ℎ with ℎ= 𝐿sin𝜃 (equivalently 𝑎= 𝑔sin𝜃 and 𝑣<sup>2</sup> = 2𝑎𝐿). (b) The collision is perfectly inelastic: momentum is conserved for the two-cart system.

answer.html: 3.41 m/s down the incline.
1.06 m/s (just after the collision, in the same direction).

check.html: The speed after sticking is less than 3.41 m/s because the moving mass is now about 3 times larger (1.90 of 6.10 kg, about 31%).

items.title: Check Your Progress, Problem 30 (Golf club and ball): A golfer swings a club and hits a golf ball. Is momentum conserved for the club and ball system? What about for the club, ball and golfer?

body.html: Momentum is conserved only when no net external force acts on the system.

answer.html: If the system is just the club and the ball, momentum is not conserved, because the golfer's hands exert an external force on the club during the hit. If the system is club + ball + golfer (+ the Earth they push on), the internal forces cancel and the total momentum is conserved. The ball's gain of momentum comes from the club (and golfer), whose momentum decreases slightly.

check.html: The club slows slightly at impact; the golfer's body keeps it moving forward.

items.title: Check Your Progress, Problem 31 (Basketball jump): A basketball player standing still jumps straight up. Where does her upward momentum come from?

body.html: Vertical momentum needs a vertical (upward) impulse from an external force.

answer.html: It comes from the floor. As she pushes down on the floor with her legs, the floor pushes up on her (Newton's third law), and the upward impulse from that force gives her upward momentum. Her own internal muscle forces alone could not change her total momentum; the outside push from the floor is required. (Earth gains a tiny equal downward momentum.)

check.html: The player alone is not an isolated system, since the floor exerts an external force.

items.title: Check Your Progress, Problem 32 (Bumper cars): Two bumper cars collide head-on and both are at rest right after the collision. Car A has mass 260 kg and was moving at 1.8 m/s. What can you say about the initial momenta of the cars, and what is the mass of car B if it was moving at 2.4 m/s?

body.html: They end at rest, so the final momentum of the two-car system is zero. Momentum is conserved during the short collision, so the initial total momentum must be zero too.

answer.html: Their initial momenta were equal in magnitude and opposite in direction: 𝑚<sub>𝐴</sub>𝑣<sub>𝐴</sub>= 𝑚<sub>𝐵</sub>𝑣<sub>𝐵</sub> (vector sum zero). The faster car was the lighter one; car B has a mass of about 2.0 × 10<sup>2</sup> kg (195 kg).

check.html: →𝑝<sub>𝐴</sub>+ →𝑝<sub>𝐵</sub>= 0, so →𝑝<sub>𝐴</sub>= −→𝑝<sub>𝐵</sub> (468 kg·m/s each).

items.title: Check Your Progress, Problem 33 (Catching a medicine ball): A 2.0-kg medicine ball is thrown horizontally at 6.0 m/s to a 58-kg person who catches it. (a) Define the system if the person stands on a rolling cart (mass 7.0 kg, wheels nearly frictionless) and if the person stands on rough pavement. (b) How does each person move after the catch?

body.html: Define the system, then ask whether the net external horizontal force is zero.
On the cart, the horizontal force from the wheels is nearly zero, so the total momentum of the system is conserved:

answer.html: On the cart, the system is person + cart + ball. The wheels roll with almost no friction, so the net external horizontal force is nearly zero. On the pavement, the system is person + ball + Earth (the ground pushes on the person's feet).

On the cart, momentum is conserved, so the person, cart and ball roll together at 0.18 m/s in the direction the ball was moving. On the pavement, static friction from the ground is an external force that cancels the ball's push. The ball's momentum is given to the person and Earth, and because Earth's mass is huge, its change in velocity is immeasurably small, so the person does not move.

check.html: Both cases obey momentum conservation; only the choice of system and the external friction differ.

items.title: 3D Thinking, Develop a Model to Illustrate: choose a propulsion technology (here, a solar sail), research how thrust is created, and model it (open-ended)

question.html: Physics idea (sample, solar sail): Light carries momentum. Each photon has momentum 𝑝= 𝐸/ 𝑐. When a mirror-like sail reflects light, the photons reverse direction, so the sail receives an impulse. For light of power 𝑃 reflected straight back, the force is 𝐹=<sub> </sub><sup>2</sup><sup>𝑃</sup> <sub>𝑐</sub>. Work (model): Draw a large, thin, reflective sail facing the Sun. Show (1) arrows of sunlight arriving, each with momentum toward the sail, (2) arrows of reflected light leaving in the opposite direction, (3) the sail's momentum arrow pointing away from the Sun, equal to the total change in the light's momentum. For example, if 1000 W of sunlight is reflected straight back:

answer.html: Model: solar sail. Reflected photons change momentum, and the sail recoils away from the Sun. The force is tiny (about 7 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>6</sup> N for 1000 W) but acts continuously and needs no fuel, so over months it builds up a large impulse.

check.html: The sketch shows light momentum reversed and a sail momentum arrow equal in size to the change in light momentum.

items.title: Focus Question: What is recoil and how is it useful?

answer.html: Recoil is the backward motion of an object when it throws something forward (a skater pushing off, a gun firing, a rocket expelling gas). Momentum is conserved, so the thrown part and the recoiling part have equal and opposite momenta. It is useful because it lets objects accelerate with nothing to push against, as rockets do in space.

items.title: Revisit the Encounter the Phenomenon Question (Lesson 2)

answer.html: Information from this lesson: a rocket and its exhaust form a closed, isolated system, so total momentum stays constant. The exhaust gains backward momentum, and the rocket gains an equal forward momentum, so it accelerates even in the vacuum of space (see Get It? below).

items.title: Figure 10, Analyze: How can you tell from the diagram that the impulses exerted by the balls have the same magnitude?

body.html: The change in momentum of each ball equals its impulse. In the diagram, the change- in-momentum arrows (𝛥𝑝<sub>𝐶</sub> and 𝛥𝑝<sub>𝐷</sub>) have equal lengths but opposite directions.

answer.html: The force vectors 𝐹<sup>D</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>C</sup> and 𝐹<sup>C</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>D</sup> are drawn with the same length (Newton's third law) and act for the same time 𝛥𝑡, so the impulses 𝐹𝛥𝑡 are equal in size and opposite in direction.

check.html: Equal and opposite impulses give equal and opposite momentum changes, so the total momentum is unchanged.

items.title: 17 (freight cars)

question.html: Two 3.0 × 10<sup>5</sup> kg freight cars collide and stick; one moves at 2.2 m/s, the other is at rest. Final speed?

body.html: 𝑚<sub>1</sub> = 𝑚<sub>2</sub> = 3.0 × 10<sup>5</sup> kg, 𝑣<sub>1</sub><sub>𝑖</sub>= + 2.2 m/s, 𝑣<sub>2</sub><sub>𝑖</sub>= 0. Find 𝑣<sub>𝑓</sub>.

The two cars form a closed, isolated system (no net external horizontal force), so momentum is conserved. In a perfectly inelastic collision, 𝑣<sub>1</sub><sub>𝑓</sub>= 𝑣<sub>2</sub><sub>𝑓</sub>= 𝑣<sub>𝑓</sub>.

answer.html: 1.1 m/s in the direction the first car was moving.

check.html: Total mass doubled, so speed is halved.

items.title: 18 (hockey puck and goalie)

question.html: A 0.105-kg puck at 24 m/s is caught by a 75-kg goalie at rest.

body.html: 𝑚<sub>𝑝</sub>= 0.105 kg, 𝑣<sub>𝑝𝑖</sub>= 24 m/s, 𝑚<sub>𝑔</sub>= 75 kg, 𝑣<sub>𝑔𝑖</sub>= 0. Find 𝑣<sub>𝑓</sub>.
Conservation of momentum for the puck + goalie system; they move together afterward.

answer.html: 0.034 m/s (3.4 cm/s) in the puck's original direction.

check.html: Tiny puck, big goalie, so a tiny recoil speed.

items.title: 19 (bullet and steel ball)

question.html: A 35.0-g bullet at 475 m/s hits a 2.5-kg steel ball at rest and bounces back at 5.0 m/s. Speed of the ball?

body.html: 𝑚<sub>𝑏</sub>= 0.0350 kg, 𝑣<sub>𝑏𝑖</sub>= + 475 m/s, 𝑣<sub>𝑏𝑓</sub>= −5.0 m/s, 𝑚<sub>𝑠</sub>= 2.5 kg, 𝑣<sub>𝑠𝑖</sub>= 0. Find 𝑣<sub>𝑠𝑓</sub>.
Momentum is conserved for the bullet + ball system.
𝑣<sub>𝑠𝑓</sub>= 𝑚<sup>𝑏</sup>(𝑣<sup>𝑏𝑖</sup>−𝑣<sup>𝑏𝑓</sup>)

answer.html: 6.7 m/s in the bullet's original direction.

check.html: The ball moves forward (the bullet gave it forward momentum and bounced back, so the ball gets more than 𝑚<sub>𝑏</sub>𝑣<sub>𝑏𝑖</sub> alone).

items.title: 20 (Challenge: head-on balls)

question.html: A 0.50-kg ball at 6.0 m/s collides head-on with a 1.00-kg ball moving the opposite way at 12.0 m/s. The 0.50-kg ball bounces backward at 14 m/s. Find the other ball's velocity.

body.html: Take the 0.50-kg ball's initial direction as +. 𝑚<sub>1</sub> = 0.50 kg, 𝑣<sub>1</sub><sub>𝑖</sub>= + 6.0 m/s, 𝑣<sub>1</sub><sub>𝑓</sub>= −14 m/s; 𝑚<sub>2</sub> = 1.00 kg, 𝑣<sub>2</sub><sub>𝑖</sub>= −12.0 m/s. Find 𝑣<sub>2</sub><sub>𝑓</sub>.
Conservation of momentum (signs matter).

answer.html: 2.0 m/s, in the direction the 1.00-kg ball was originally moving (the negative direction, same direction as the 0.50-kg ball's rebound).

check.html: Initial momentum = −9.0; final = −7.0 + ( −2.0) = −9.0 kg·m/s. Matches.

items.title: Figure 11, Infer: How can you tell from the motion that the boy's mass is greater than the girl's mass?

body.html: After the push, 𝑚<sub>𝐶</sub>𝑣<sub>𝐶</sub>= −𝑚<sub>𝐷</sub>𝑣<sub>𝐷</sub> (equal and opposite momenta), so the one with the smaller speed has the larger mass.

answer.html: The girl moves farther forward than the boy moves backward in the same time, so the girl's speed is larger. Since their momenta are equal in size, the boy must have the larger mass.

check.html: 𝑚<sub>𝐶</sub>/ 𝑚<sub>𝐷</sub>= 𝑣<sub>𝐷</sub>/ 𝑣<sub>𝐶</sub>> 1.

items.title: Systems and System Models (Crosscutting Concepts, Figure 11)

body.html: To use conservation of momentum, you must define the system and know the velocities relative to a frame that is not accelerating. The red ball sits on the floor and does not move, so it marks a fixed reference position.

The ball lets you see how far each skater moved relative to the ground: the girl moves forward, the boy backward. This shows that their displacements (and velocities) have opposite directions and different sizes, so you can compare their speeds and infer masses. Another way: mark the floor with tape and measure positions at equal time intervals, or use a motion detector or a video with a meter stick in view. Model: a diagram with the two skaters as a system (dashed boundary), 𝑝<sub>before</sub> = 0, and arrows after the push for →𝑝<sub>𝐶</sub> (left) and →𝑝<sub>𝐷</sub> (right) of equal length.

answer.html: The red ball provides a fixed reference so you can measure each skater's displacement and therefore their speeds. Tape marks on the floor or a video grid would also work. The model: system = both skaters, total momentum zero before and after, with equal and opposite momentum arrows.

check.html: The arrows sum to zero, as they should.

items.title: Get It? (Lesson 2, "Propulsion in Space"): Explain how the rocket at the start of the module can accelerate in space.

answer.html: The rocket and its fuel form a closed, isolated system. Burning fuel makes hot gas that is pushed out the nozzle backward at high speed. The gas gains backward momentum, so by conservation of momentum (and Newton's third law) the rocket gains an equal forward momentum, and so it accelerates, with nothing outside to push against.

check.html: Matches Example Problem 4 (astronaut and gas).

items.title: 21 (model rocket)

question.html: A 4.00-kg model rocket expels 50.0 g of burned fuel at 625 m/s. Find the rocket's velocity after the fuel burns (ignore gravity and air).

body.html: 𝑚<sub>𝑟</sub>= 4.00 kg (rocket, as the problem states), 𝑚<sub>𝑔</sub>= 0.0500 kg, 𝑣<sub>𝑔𝑓</sub>= −625 m/s (backward), initial momentum = 0.
Momentum conservation, as in Example Problem 4: 0 = 𝑚<sub>𝑟</sub>𝑣<sub>𝑟</sub>+ 𝑚<sub>𝑔</sub>𝑣<sub>𝑔</sub>.

answer.html: 7.81 m/s in the direction opposite to the exhaust (forward). If you instead use the rocket's mass after burn-out (3.95 kg) you get 7.91 m/s; the book's setup (4.00 kg) gives 7.81 m/s.

check.html: Direction opposite to the gas; speed much less than 625 m/s since the rocket is far heavier.

items.title: 22 (two carts and a spring)

question.html: A spring pushes apart a 1.5-kg cart and a 4.5-kg cart (initially at rest, tied together). The 1.5-kg cart moves at 27 m/s left. Velocity of the 4.5-kg cart?

body.html: Right is +. 𝑚<sub>1</sub> = 1.5 kg, 𝑣<sub>1</sub><sub>𝑓</sub>= −27 m/s, 𝑚<sub>2</sub> = 4.5 kg. Initial momentum 0.
Conservation of momentum for the two carts (spring force is internal).
0 = 𝑚<sub>1</sub>𝑣<sub>1</sub><sub>𝑓</sub>+ 𝑚<sub>2</sub>𝑣<sub>2</sub><sub>𝑓</sub>

answer.html: 9.0 m/s to the right (opposite the 1.5-kg cart).

check.html: The cart three times heavier moves at one third the speed.

items.title: 23 (Challenge: canoe)

question.html: Carmen (80.0 kg) steps from the canoe onto the dock at 4.0 m/s forward. The canoe and Judi (combined 115 kg) were at rest. Speed and direction of the canoe?

body.html: Forward is +. 𝑚<sub>𝐶</sub>= 80.0 kg, 𝑣<sub>𝐶</sub><sub>𝑓</sub>= + 4.0 m/s, 𝑚<sub>𝐽</sub>= 115 kg (canoe + Judi). Initial momentum 0 (the canoe is free to move on the water).
Momentum conservation for Carmen + canoe + Judi.
0 = 𝑚<sub>𝐶</sub>𝑣<sub>𝐶</sub><sub>𝑓</sub>+ 𝑚<sub>𝐽</sub>𝑣<sub>𝐽𝑓</sub>

answer.html: 2.8 m/s backward (opposite to Carmen's motion).

check.html: Carmen is lighter than the canoe plus Judi, so the canoe's speed is lower than 4.0 m/s.

items.title: Figure 12, Analyze: why is momentum of the three balls not conserved on high-friction carpet?

body.html: Momentum of a system is conserved only if the net external force is zero. Carpet friction is an external force on the balls.

answer.html: Friction from the carpet exerts an external force on the balls, so the three balls (system) lose momentum. That momentum goes to the carpet/Earth, which gains an equal momentum in the opposite sense (a tiny change since Earth is so massive), so total momentum of the larger system (balls + carpet + Earth) is conserved.

check.html: Balls slow down and stop on carpet; their lost momentum is exactly the momentum given to the Earth.

items.title: 24 (north car and west car)

question.html: A 925-kg car moving north at 20.1 m/s hits a 1865-kg car moving west at 13.4 m/s; they stick.

body.html: North = +y, west = +x (so both components positive). 𝑝<sub>𝑁</sub>= (925)(20.1), 𝑝<sub>𝑊</sub>= (1865)(13.4); total mass 2790 kg. Find 𝑣<sub>𝑓</sub> and direction.
Momentum is conserved separately along each axis; the final momentum is the vector sum.
𝑝<sup>𝑓</sup>= √𝑝<sup>𝑥</sup>

answer.html: 11.2 m/s, 36.6° north of west.

check.html: The heavier car was moving west, so the result points mostly west; the speed is below both initial speeds' maximum (20.1 m/s).

items.title: 25 (south car struck by east car)

question.html: A 1383-kg car moving south at 11.2 m/s is struck by a 1732-kg car moving east at 31.3 m/s; they stick.

body.html: East = +x, south = +y (down the page), total mass 3115 kg.
Same as above: add momentum components.

answer.html: 18.1 m/s, 15.9° south of east.

check.html: Mostly eastward because the east-moving car has much more momentum.

items.title: 26 (was the north-moving car speeding?)

question.html: A 1345-kg car moving east at 15.7 m/s is struck by a 1923-kg car moving north. They stick and move at 14.5 m/s at 𝜃= 63.5° (north of east). Was the north-moving car over the 20.1 m/s limit?

body.html: East = +x, north = +y. 𝑚<sub>𝐸</sub>= 1345 kg, 𝑣<sub>𝐸</sub>= 15.7 m/s, 𝑚<sub>𝑁</sub>= 1923 kg, 𝑣<sub>𝑓</sub>= 14.5 m/s, 𝜃= 63.5°, total mass 3268 kg. Find 𝑣<sub>𝑁</sub>.
The initial north momentum belongs only to the north car and must equal the final y- momentum.
Check with the x-direction: (3268)(14.5)cos63.5° = 2.11 × 10<sup>4</sup> and (1345)(15.7) = 2.11 × 10<sup>4</sup> kg·m/s. They agree.

answer.html: Yes. The north-moving car was going about 22 m/s, which exceeds the 20.1 m/s limit.

check.html: The x-momentum matches, so the given data are consistent.

items.title: 27 (Challenge: billiard balls)

question.html: A 0.17-kg ball moving 4.0 m/s strikes an identical ball at rest. The moving ball leaves 60.0° to the left of its original direction; the other ball leaves 30.0° to the right. Find the velocity of each.

body.html: 𝑚= 0.17 kg for both, 𝑣<sub>𝑖</sub>= 4.0 m/s along +x. Final angles: +60.0° (ball 1, left) and −30.0° (ball 2, right). Find 𝑣<sub>1</sub><sub>𝑓</sub>, 𝑣<sub>2</sub><sub>𝑓</sub>.
Conservation of momentum in x and y separately (the identical mass cancels).
y-direction (initial 𝑝<sub>𝑦</sub>= 0): 𝑣<sub>1</sub><sub>𝑓</sub>sin60.0° −𝑣<sub>2</sub><sub>𝑓</sub>sin30.0° = 0
x-direction: 𝑣<sub>𝑖</sub>= 𝑣<sub>1</sub><sub>𝑓</sub>cos60.0° + 𝑣<sub>2</sub><sub>𝑓</sub>cos30.0° = 𝑣<sub>1</sub><sub>𝑓</sub>(0.500 + 1.732 × 0.866) = 2.00 𝑣<sub>1</sub><sub>𝑓</sub>

answer.html: The ball originally moving: 2.0 m/s at 60.0° left of its original direction. The ball originally at rest: 3.5 m/s at 30.0° to the right.

check.html: Kinetic energy: <sub>12</sub>𝑚(2.0<sup>2</sup> + 3.46<sup>2</sup>) =<sub> </sub><sub>12</sub>𝑚(16), equal to the initial <sub>12</sub>𝑚(4.0<sup>2</sup>), so this is an elastic collision.

items.title: Figure 14, Decide: Why does the top precess only when it is tilted?

body.html: Torque = (lever arm) × (force). When the top is vertical, gravity acts along a line through the pivot, so the lever arm is zero and there is no torque. Tilted, gravity acts at the center of mass off the vertical line through the pivot, giving a torque perpendicular to → 𝐿.

answer.html: A vertical top has zero torque (gravity acts through the pivot), so its angular momentum does not change. When tilted, gravity gives a torque that changes the direction of → 𝐿 (not its size), so the axis sweeps around the vertical: precession.

check.html: Torque perpendicular to → 𝐿 turns → 𝐿 rather than speeding or slowing the spin.

items.title: Get It? (Tops and Gyroscopes): Why does Earth precess as it rotates?

answer.html: Earth has an equatorial bulge and its axis is tilted, so the Sun's (and Moon's) gravitational pull on the bulge exerts a small torque. Because Earth has large angular momentum, the torque changes the direction of the axis slowly (a cycle takes about 26,000 years) instead of tipping it over.

check.html: Same mechanism as the tilted top.

items.title: Physics Challenge: Colliding Cars

question.html: A 1265-kg car heading north is hit by a 925-kg car heading west. They stick and slide 23.1 m at 42° north of west. Speed limit 22 m/s. 𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>= 0.65.

body.html: From Figure (read): axes +x east, +y north; the combined wreck moves 42° north of west. 𝑚<sub>𝑁</sub>= 1265 kg (north car, your friend), 𝑚<sub>𝑊</sub>= 925 kg (west car), 𝑀= 2190 kg, skid distance 𝑑= 23.1 m, 𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>= 0.65, 𝑔= 9.80 m/s<sup>2</sup>. Find 𝑣<sub>𝑁</sub> and 𝑣<sub>𝑊</sub> before the crash.
(1) During the skid, friction is the only horizontal force: 𝑎= 𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>𝑔 and 𝑣<sub>𝑓</sub>
gives the speed right after impact. (2) Momentum is conserved in the collision along each axis.
Speed just after the collision (skid to rest):
North momentum before = north momentum after: 𝑚<sub>𝑁</sub>𝑣<sub>𝑁</sub>= 𝑀𝑣sin42°
West momentum before = west momentum after: 𝑚<sub>𝑊</sub>𝑣<sub>𝑊</sub>= 𝑀𝑣cos42°

answer.html: Your friend (north car) was going about 20 m/s (19.9 m/s), under the 22 m/s limit.
The other car (west) was going about 30 m/s (30.2 m/s), well over the limit. Yes, the evidence supports your friend's claim: she was not speeding and the other driver was.

check.html: The west car has less mass but much more speed, so its momentum is larger, which is why the wreck slides toward the west more than north.

items.title: Check Your Progress, Problem 28 (thick, heavy rim on a plastic disk)

body.html: Moment of inertia 𝐼= ∑𝑚𝑟<sup>2</sup> is large when mass is far from the axis. Angular momentum 𝐿= 𝐼𝜔.

answer.html: A heavy rim puts most of the mass far from the axis, giving a large moment of inertia. For a given spin rate the disk has a large angular momentum, so it resists changes in its spin axis (it acts like a gyroscope) and flies steadily without wobbling.

check.html: Same idea as the gyroscope and the spiral football.

items.title: Check Your Progress, Problem 29 (carts on a ramp, Figure 16)

question.html: A 24.5-N cart is released from rest on a 1.00-m ramp at 30.0° and strikes a 36.8-N cart at the bottom. (a) Speed of the first cart at the bottom. (b) Speed if they stick together.

body.html: Reading Figure 16: ramp length 1.00 m, angle 30.0°, cart 1 weighs 24.5 N, cart 2 weighs 36.8 N and is next to the bottom of the ramp (assumed at rest). Masses: 𝑚<sub>1</sub> = 24.5 / 9.80 = 2.50 kg, 𝑚<sub>2</sub> = 36.8 / 9.80 = 3.76 kg. Assume no friction (a frictionless ramp).

(a) On a frictionless incline, the speed at the bottom follows from energy conservation: <sub>12</sub>𝑚𝑣<sup>2</sup> = 𝑚𝑔ℎ with ℎ= 𝐿sin𝜃 (equivalently 𝑎= 𝑔sin𝜃 and 𝑣<sup>2</sup> = 2𝑎𝐿). (b) The collision is perfectly inelastic: momentum is conserved for the two-cart system.

answer.html: 3.13 m/s down the incline.
1.25 m/s (just after the collision, in the same direction).

check.html: The speed after sticking is less than 3.13 m/s because the mass has increased (2.50 of 6.26 kg, about 40%).

items.title: Check Your Progress, Problem 30 (tennis racket and ball)

body.html: Momentum is conserved only when no net external force acts on the system.

answer.html: If the system is just the racket and the ball, momentum is not conserved because the player's hand exerts an external force on the racket during the hit (that is why the racket keeps moving forward). If the system is racket + ball + player (+ the Earth they push on), the internal forces cancel, and total momentum is conserved. The ball's gain of momentum comes from the racket (and player), whose momentum decreases slightly.

check.html: Racket slows slightly when it hits the ball; a heavy racket+arm keeps moving.

items.title: Check Your Progress, Problem 31 (pole-vaulter's vertical momentum)

body.html: Vertical momentum needs a vertical (upward) impulse from an external force.

answer.html: It comes from the ground and the pole. When the vaulter plants the pole in the box, the pole bends and pushes back on the vaulter; the upward component of that force (and the push of the ground) gives an upward impulse that turns part of the horizontal momentum into vertical motion. The vaulter's own horizontal momentum does not become vertical momentum by itself; an outside force is required.

check.html: The system (vaulter alone) is not isolated, since the pole and ground exert external forces.

items.title: Check Your Progress, Problem 32 (soccer players colliding and stopping)

body.html: They come to rest together, so the final momentum of the two-player system is zero. If momentum is conserved (during the short collision), the initial total momentum must be zero too.

answer.html: Their initial momenta were equal in magnitude and opposite in direction: 𝑚<sub>1</sub>𝑣<sub>1</sub> = 𝑚<sub>2</sub>𝑣<sub>2</sub> (vector sum zero). The heavier player was moving more slowly.

check.html: →𝑝<sub>1</sub> + →𝑝<sub>2</sub> = 0, so →𝑝<sub>1</sub> = −→𝑝<sub>2</sub>.

items.title: Check Your Progress, Problem 33 (catching a ball on a skateboard vs. on the ground)

body.html: Define the system, then ask whether the net external horizontal force is zero.

answer.html: On the skateboard, the system is you + skateboard + ball. The wheels roll with almost no friction, so the net external horizontal force is nearly zero. On the ground, the system is you + ball + Earth (the ground pushes on your feet).
On the skateboard, momentum is conserved: the ball's momentum before the catch equals the total momentum of (you + board + ball) after, so 𝑣=

<sub>𝑚</sub><sub>ball</sub><sub> +</sub><sub> 𝑚</sub><sub>you</sub><sub> +</sub><sub> 𝑚</sub><sub>board</sub> in the ball's direction, so you roll (in the direction the ball was moving, which is backward from your facing direction if it was thrown toward you). On the ground, static friction from the ground exerts an external force that cancels the ball's push; the ball's momentum is given to you and Earth, and because Earth's mass is huge, the change in its velocity is immeasurably small, so you do not move.

check.html: Both cases obey momentum conservation; only the system choice and external friction differ.

items.title: 3D Thinking, Develop a Model to Illustrate: choose a propulsion technology, research how thrust is created, and model it (open-ended)

question.html: Physics idea (sample, ion thruster): An ion thruster uses electric fields to accelerate ions to very high speed and expel them out the back. By conservation of momentum, the spacecraft gains an equal momentum forward. Thrust is 𝐹=<sub> </sub><sup>𝛥</sup><sup>𝑝</sup> <sub>𝛥</sub><sub>𝑡</sub>= ˙𝑚𝑣<sub>exhaust</sub> (mass of ions per second times exhaust speed). Work (model): Draw the spacecraft as a box with a thruster at the rear. Show (1) a gas source feeding ions, (2) charged grids with an electric field accelerating ions backward at speed 𝑣<sub>𝑒</sub>, (3) arrows: ion momentum backward, spacecraft momentum forward, equal in size. Label: 𝑚<sub>craft</sub>𝑣<sub>craft</sub> = 𝑚<sub>ions</sub>𝑣<sub>ions</sub> (zero total initial momentum).

answer.html: Model: ion thruster. Ions are accelerated backward by an electric field; the craft recoils forward. Thrust = ˙𝑚𝑣<sub>𝑒</sub>: small force but sustained for a long time, which builds up a large impulse. (A solar sail works because photons carry momentum 𝑝= 𝐸/ 𝑐 and give an impulse when reflected.)

check.html: The sketch shows equal and opposite momentum arrows.
